Asthma is a chronic condition in which the airways become inflamed, narrowed, and produce extra mucus, making breathing difficult. Unlike COPD, asthma's airflow limitation is typically reversible, either on its own or with medication, and it often begins in childhood, though it can develop at any age. Common triggers include allergens (pollen, dust mites, pet dander, mold), respiratory infections, cold air, exercise, air pollution, strong odors, and stress. During an asthma attack, the muscles around the airways tighten (bronchospasm) and the airway lining swells and produces mucus, all of which narrow the space air can pass through. Typical symptoms include wheezing (a whistling sound when breathing), shortness of breath, chest tightness, and coughing, which is often worse at night or early in the morning. Severity ranges widely: some people have mild, infrequent symptoms, while others experience frequent flare-ups that significantly affect daily life. Asthma is usually managed with two categories of medication: quick-relief (rescue) inhalers, typically short-acting bronchodilators used during an attack to rapidly open the airways, and long-term control medications, often inhaled corticosteroids, taken regularly to reduce underlying airway inflammation and prevent attacks from happening in the first place. An asthma action plan, developed with a healthcare provider, helps patients recognize worsening symptoms early and know when to adjust medication or seek emergency care. Severe, uncontrolled asthma attacks can be life-threatening and require immediate medical attention.
Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes, the airways that carry air to and from the lungs, and it comes in two main forms: acute and chronic. Acute bronchitis is usually caused by the same viruses responsible for colds and the flu, develops over a few days, and typically resolves within one to three weeks as the body clears the infection; antibiotics generally aren't helpful since the cause is viral, not bacterial. Chronic bronchitis, on the other hand, is a long-term condition defined by a persistent productive cough lasting at least three months a year for two consecutive years, and it's actually classified as one of the two main forms of COPD, most often caused by long-term smoking or exposure to lung irritants. Symptoms of acute bronchitis include a cough that may produce clear, yellow, or greenish mucus, chest discomfort, mild fever, fatigue, and sometimes wheezing or shortness of breath. Chronic bronchitis shares these symptoms but persists or recurs over months and years, and often worsens gradually. Management for acute bronchitis is mainly supportive: rest, fluids, and over-the-counter symptom relief, since it usually clears on its own. Chronic bronchitis management focuses on the same strategies used for COPD more broadly — smoking cessation being the most important step, along with bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and pulmonary rehabilitation to manage symptoms and slow progression.
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a long-term, progressive lung condition that makes it hard to breathe due to narrowed or damaged airways and air sacs. It's actually an umbrella term that mainly covers two related conditions: chronic bronchitis (long-term inflammation and mucus buildup in the airways) and emphysema (damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs that reduces their ability to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide efficiently). The overwhelming majority of COPD cases are caused by long-term exposure to irritants that damage the lungs, with cigarette smoking being the leading cause; long-term exposure to air pollution, chemical fumes, or dust can also contribute, especially in combination with smoking. Symptoms usually develop gradually and worsen over time, including chronic cough (often with mucus), wheezing, shortness of breath — especially during physical activity — chest tightness, and frequent respiratory infections. Unlike asthma, COPD-related airflow limitation is not usually fully reversible, though treatment can slow its progression and improve quality of life. There is no cure for COPD, but management typically includes quitting smoking (the single most impactful intervention), bronchodilator medications to relax airway muscles, inhaled corticosteroids to reduce inflammation, pulmonary rehabilitation programs, and supplemental oxygen therapy in more advanced cases. Flare-ups, called exacerbations, can be triggered by respiratory infections or air pollution and may require more intensive treatment.
COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, primarily affects the respiratory system, though it can impact other organs as well. It spreads mainly through respiratory droplets and aerosols released when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs, or sneezes. The severity of respiratory involvement varies widely: many infections cause mild, cold-like or flu-like symptoms, while others progress to viral pneumonia, and in severe cases, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a life-threatening condition in which the lungs become severely inflamed and fill with fluid, drastically impairing oxygen exchange. Common respiratory symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and in more severe cases, dangerously low blood oxygen levels that may not always correspond to how short of breath the person feels (a phenomenon sometimes called "silent hypoxia"). Risk factors for severe respiratory illness include older age, obesity, chronic lung disease (like COPD or asthma), heart disease, diabetes, and a weakened immune system. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through PCR or antigen testing, with chest imaging (CT or X-ray) sometimes used to assess the extent of lung involvement in more severe cases. Management ranges from supportive care (rest, fluids, fever reducers) for mild cases to supplemental oxygen, antiviral medications, corticosteroids to reduce lung inflammation, and mechanical ventilation in the most severe cases. Vaccination has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of severe respiratory illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19.
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which affects the movement of salt and water in and out of cells. This leads to the production of unusually thick, sticky mucus that can clog the airways in the lungs and block ducts in other organs, particularly the pancreas. It's an inherited condition — a person needs to receive a mutated copy of the gene from both parents to have CF — and it's typically diagnosed in infancy or early childhood, often through newborn screening programs in many countries. In the lungs, the thick mucus makes it difficult to clear bacteria, leading to frequent and sometimes severe lung infections, chronic cough, wheezing, and progressive lung damage over time. Beyond the respiratory system, CF commonly affects digestion, since thick mucus can block the ducts that carry digestive enzymes from the pancreas to the intestines, leading to poor nutrient absorption, and it can also affect fertility. There is no cure for CF, but treatment has advanced substantially in recent decades, including airway clearance techniques to help loosen and clear mucus, inhaled medications to thin mucus and fight infection, pancreatic enzyme replacement to aid digestion, and — more recently — a class of drugs called CFTR modulators that target the underlying genetic defect itself in patients with specific mutations, significantly improving lung function and quality of life for many. With ongoing advances in care, life expectancy for people with CF has increased substantially over the past several decades.
Lung cancer occurs when cells in the lung grow uncontrollably, forming tumors that can interfere with normal lung function and potentially spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body. It is broadly divided into two main types: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for the large majority of cases and tends to grow more slowly, and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), which is less common but typically more aggressive and fast-growing. Cigarette smoking is the leading risk factor by a wide margin, but other contributors include secondhand smoke exposure, radon gas exposure, occupational exposure to substances like asbestos, air pollution, and a family history of lung cancer. Early-stage lung cancer often causes no symptoms, which is part of why it's frequently diagnosed at a later stage. When symptoms do appear, they can include a persistent cough that worsens over time, coughing up blood, chest pain, hoarseness, unexplained weight loss, shortness of breath, and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia. Diagnosis typically involves imaging (chest X-ray or CT scan), followed by a biopsy to confirm cancer cells and determine the specific type. Treatment options depend heavily on the type and stage at diagnosis, and can include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted drug therapy, and immunotherapy. Screening with low-dose CT scans is recommended for some high-risk individuals, such as long-term heavy smokers within a certain age range, because catching lung cancer earlier significantly improves treatment outcomes.
Pleurisy (also called pleuritis) is inflammation of the pleura, the two thin layers of tissue that line the outside of the lungs and the inside of the chest cavity. Normally, a small amount of fluid between these layers allows them to slide smoothly against each other as the lungs expand and contract during breathing. When the pleura becomes inflamed, the layers can rub against each other roughly, causing sharp chest pain, especially when breathing deeply, coughing, or sneezing. Pleurisy has many possible causes, including viral infections (the most common cause), bacterial pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, autoimmune conditions like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, and less commonly, lung cancer or tuberculosis. The hallmark symptom is a sharp, stabbing chest pain that typically worsens with breathing, coughing, or movement, and may improve when holding one's breath or lying on the affected side. Other symptoms can include shortness of breath, cough, and fever if an underlying infection is present. In some cases, fluid can accumulate in the space between the pleural layers, a condition called a pleural effusion, which can cause additional shortness of breath and may require drainage if significant. Diagnosis involves a physical exam (a doctor listening for a distinctive "rubbing" sound with a stethoscope), chest X-ray, and sometimes blood tests or imaging to identify the underlying cause. Treatment focuses on addressing that underlying cause, along with pain relief and anti-inflammatory medication to manage symptoms in the meantime.
Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs, causing them to fill with fluid or pus. It can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi, and the cause affects how it's treated: bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics, while viral pneumonia typically resolves with supportive care since antibiotics don't work against viruses. Common symptoms include cough (often producing phlegm), fever, chills, difficulty breathing, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, and fatigue. In young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems, pneumonia can become severe quickly and may require hospitalization. Diagnosis usually involves a physical exam (listening to the lungs), a chest X-ray to confirm fluid or consolidation in the lung tissue, and sometimes blood tests or sputum cultures to identify the causative organism. Risk factors include smoking, chronic lung disease, a weakened immune system, and recent viral respiratory infections like the flu. Vaccines exist for some of the most common bacterial causes (such as Streptococcus pneumoniae) and are recommended for young children, older adults, and people with certain chronic conditions. Someone with pneumonia should seek medical attention if they have difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, a high fever, or confusion, as these can signal a more serious case.
A pulmonary embolism (PE) is a sudden blockage in one of the pulmonary arteries in the lungs, usually caused by a blood clot that has traveled from elsewhere in the body — most commonly the deep veins of the legs, a condition called deep vein thrombosis (DVT). When a clot breaks loose and travels through the bloodstream to the lungs, it can partially or completely block blood flow, which is a medical emergency. Risk factors include prolonged immobility (such as long flights or bed rest after surgery), certain surgeries, cancer, pregnancy, hormone therapy or birth control pills, smoking, obesity, and inherited clotting disorders. Symptoms can develop suddenly and include shortness of breath (often the most prominent symptom), sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing, rapid heart rate, coughing (sometimes with blood-tinged sputum), lightheadedness, or fainting. A large PE can be life-threatening very quickly because it prevents oxygen from reaching the bloodstream efficiently and puts sudden strain on the heart. Diagnosis often involves a CT pulmonary angiogram, blood tests (like a D-dimer test), and sometimes an ultrasound of the legs to check for DVT. Treatment typically centers on blood-thinning medication (anticoagulants) to prevent the clot from growing and allow the body to gradually dissolve it, and in severe cases, clot-dissolving drugs or procedures to physically remove the clot may be needed. Anyone experiencing sudden shortness of breath with chest pain should seek emergency care immediately, since prompt treatment significantly improves outcomes.
Pulmonary fibrosis is a condition in which lung tissue becomes scarred and thickened over time, making it increasingly difficult for oxygen to pass from the lungs into the bloodstream. The scarring is generally irreversible, and as it progresses, the lungs become stiffer and less able to expand fully, leading to progressively worsening shortness of breath. In many cases, no specific cause can be identified, a form known as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), which tends to affect older adults and progresses at a variable but generally steady pace. Known causes and contributing factors in other cases include long-term exposure to certain dusts or chemicals (such as asbestos or silica), certain autoimmune diseases (like rheumatoid arthritis or scleroderma), some medications, radiation therapy to the chest, and chronic conditions like gastroesophageal reflux disease. Symptoms typically develop gradually and include shortness of breath — especially during physical activity — a persistent dry cough, fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and widening/rounding of the fingertips and nails (a sign called clubbing) in more advanced cases. Diagnosis usually involves a combination of a high-resolution CT scan of the chest, pulmonary function tests to measure lung capacity, and sometimes a lung biopsy to characterize the scarring pattern. While there's no cure that reverses existing scarring, treatments including antifibrotic medications can slow disease progression, and pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental oxygen, and in eligible patients, lung transplantation, can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life.
Sleep apnea is a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep, and the most common form, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), occurs when the muscles in the back of the throat relax excessively and block the airway. A less common form, central sleep apnea, happens when the brain fails to send proper signals to the muscles that control breathing. Each pause in breathing, called an apnea, can last from a few seconds to over a minute and may happen dozens or even hundreds of times a night in more severe cases, though the person is often unaware it's happening. Common symptoms include loud snoring, gasping or choking sounds during sleep, waking up with a dry mouth or sore throat, morning headaches, excessive daytime sleepiness even after a full night's sleep, difficulty concentrating, and irritability. Risk factors include excess weight (particularly around the neck), a naturally narrow airway, enlarged tonsils, smoking, alcohol use, and family history. Left untreated, sleep apnea is associated with an increased risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes, largely because the repeated drops in blood oxygen levels put ongoing strain on the cardiovascular system. Diagnosis is typically confirmed with a sleep study, either in a sleep lab or with a home testing device, which monitors breathing patterns, oxygen levels, and other measures overnight. Treatment options range from lifestyle changes (weight loss, avoiding alcohol before bed, sleeping on one's side) to CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machines, which are the most common and effective treatment for moderate to severe OSA, and in some cases oral appliances or surgery.
Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that most commonly affects the lungs, though it can spread to other organs as well. It spreads through the air when a person with active TB disease coughs, speaks, or sings, releasing tiny droplets that others can inhale. Importantly, TB infection exists on a spectrum: in latent TB infection, the bacteria are present in the body but inactive, causing no symptoms and being non-contagious, while in active TB disease, the bacteria are actively multiplying and causing illness, and the person can spread it to others. Symptoms of active pulmonary TB typically include a persistent cough lasting three weeks or longer (sometimes with blood), chest pain, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, and loss of appetite. Diagnosis involves a combination of skin or blood tests to check for TB infection, chest X-rays to look for lung involvement, and sputum tests to confirm active disease and identify the specific bacterial strain. Treatment for active TB requires a lengthy course of multiple antibiotics, typically taken for six to nine months, and it's critical to complete the full course even after symptoms improve — stopping early is a major driver of drug-resistant TB strains, which are much harder to treat. TB remains a significant global health issue, particularly in regions with limited healthcare access, and is closely linked to factors like overcrowding, malnutrition, and weakened immune systems (including HIV co-infection).
